planting.note: Set out after the soil has warmed, since the long taproot resents disturbance once established.

directions: Choose a lean, gritty, sharply drained site, since rich soil produces floppy growth and dulls the steel-blue color. Skip winter mulch over the crown in cold climates, as excess moisture around the roots is more damaging than the cold itself. Cut stems for fresh or dried arrangements once the bracts fully color, and deadhead spent flowers to extend the bloom window into fall. Bees and other pollinators work the thistle-like flower heads heavily during peak bloom.
sources: University of Washington Botanic Gardens plant profile series

planting.note: Give it the sunniest spot available, since foliage color and flower blue intensity both depend on strong light.

directions: This compact clump-former is grown as much for chartreuse-to-gold foliage as for its electric-blue, silver-to-lavender-bracted flowers, so pair it where both traits show against darker neighbors. Plant in dry, sandy, well-drained soil, since wet feet in winter are its main threat in colder zones. Established clumps are quite drought tolerant and rarely need staking. Leave seed heads standing into winter for structure and for goldfinches and other seed-eating birds.

planting.note: Give this selection extra room at planting time, since it forms a substantial clump of towering, self-supporting stems by its second season.

directions: Selected in Jonesboro, Arkansas for stems that stay upright without staking despite the plant's imposing height, unlike many wild giant ironweed clones that flop under their own flower weight. Site it at the back of a border or in a meadow planting with consistently moist, fertile soil and full sun. Deep purple flower clusters open in late summer and draw heavy butterfly and native bee traffic right through into fall. Cut stems back in late winter before new growth emerges to keep the clump tidy.
sources: Plant Delights Nursery / Juniper Level Botanic Garden catalog notes
Chicago Botanic Garden comparative ironweed evaluation

planting.note: Plant in consistently moist soil, since this bushier selection still wants the damp footing typical of spotted Joe-Pye weed.

directions: This denser, more compact selection holds its purple-flushed, red-dashed stems upright without staking, making it easier to place near the middle of a border than the straight species. Red-purple stems and bronze-tinted terminal leaves give it multi-season interest before the loose, dusty-pink flower domes open in late summer. It shows good resistance to powdery mildew compared with many Joe-Pye weed relatives. Leave seed heads standing through fall for songbirds and overwintering beneficial insects.
sources: Chicago Botanic Garden comparative Joe-Pye weed evaluation

planting.note: Reserve a spot at the back of the bed, since 'Riesenschirm' (German for giant umbrella) is one of the tallest Joe-Pye weed selections available.

directions: Slender but sturdy burgundy stems carry flat, 8-to-12-inch domes of dusky pink flowers from midsummer into fall without needing to be staked, even in wind and rain. Plant in deep, humus-rich soil that stays evenly moist, matching the wet meadows this species favors in the wild. The RHS Award of Garden Merit reflects its reliability and outstanding pollinator appeal. Fluffy seed heads extend interest well into winter and feed songbirds after the flowers fade.
